reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Characterised by a midline facial malformation with widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), a broad nasal root, and midline defects of the nose and upper lip
Features may include a median cleft of the nose or lip, a widow's peak hairline, and a bifid nasal tip
It reflects abnormal development of the frontonasal prominence, from which the central face derives
Severity ranges from mild hypertelorism to severe midline clefting with anterior cranium bifidum
It may be isolated or form part of defined syndromes, some caused by variants in the ALX family of genes
Associated midline brain anomalies can occur, so intracranial imaging is important when clefting is significant
The degree of cognitive involvement varies and often relates to accompanying central nervous system malformation rather than the facial defect alone
reference.pathophysiology: Frontonasal dysplasia arises from disturbed development of the frontonasal prominence, the midline facial process that gives rise to the forehead, nasal bridge, nasal tip, philtrum, and primary palate. Failure of the medial nasal processes to migrate and merge normally in the midline results in the widened, clefted central face and hypertelorism. Because midline facial and forebrain development are intimately linked, disruption in this region can be accompanied by midline central nervous system anomalies. Several genetic forms are recognised, notably those due to variants in the ALX homeobox genes governing craniofacial midline patterning, though many cases are sporadic and aetiologically heterogeneous.
additionalDifferentials: Holoprosencephaly spectrum (with hypotelorism at the severe end)
Median cleft lip from other causes
Encephalocele or nasal glioma presenting with a midline mass
additionalInvestigations: Cranial magnetic resonance imaging to detect midline brain anomalies and distinguish encephalocele
Craniofacial computed tomography to define the bony defect for surgical planning
Ophthalmological assessment of orbital position and vision
Molecular testing including ALX-related genes where indicated
Genetic counselling based on the specific diagnosis identified
redFlags: A midline nasal mass that may represent an encephalocele with a risk of cerebrospinal fluid leak or meningitis
Associated significant central nervous system malformation
Visual compromise from severe orbital displacement
Airway concerns where nasal anatomy is markedly abnormal
Features indicating a broader syndrome requiring multisystem evaluation
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the extent of facial clefting and, crucially, on any associated brain malformation; isolated milder forms have a good prognosis with staged reconstruction and normal cognition, whereas central nervous system involvement worsens developmental outlook.
pitfalls: Biopsying or operating on a midline nasal mass before excluding an encephalocele
Attributing all developmental concern to the facial appearance rather than to brain anomalies
Failing to obtain intracranial imaging in significant midline clefting
Overlooking the genetic heterogeneity and the need for tailored counselling
Assuming hypertelorism is purely cosmetic without assessing vision and orbital anatomy
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
management: Staged craniofacial surgical reconstruction to correct the midline cleft, hypertelorism and nasal deformity, timed to facial growth
Neonatal assessment and support of feeding and airway where midline clefting is significant
Intracranial imaging and neurosurgical management of any associated midline brain anomaly or encephalocele
Ophthalmological assessment and management of orbital malposition and visual function
Developmental assessment and support, with intervention where central nervous system involvement affects cognition
Multidisciplinary craniofacial team care coordinating plastic surgery, neurosurgery, ophthalmology and genetics
Genetic counselling based on the specific diagnosis, including ALX-related recessive forms where identified
